wiki.content: Super Trouper is the seventh studio album by the Swedish pop group ABBA, released on 3 November 1980. It features the No.1 singles "The Winner Takes It All" and "Super Trouper". The album became the biggest-selling album of 1980 in the UK. Overview Led by the international hit "The Winner Takes It All", Super Trouper was the group's sixth chart-topping album in the UK. It was also the best-selling album in Britain for 1980. Super Trouper was first released on CD in 1983 by Polar Music International, in the early 1980s by Polydor, and in the late 1980s by Atlantic Records for the US. The album has been reissued in digitally remastered form four times; first in 1997, then in 2001, again in 2005 as part of The Complete Studio Recordings box set and as a Deluxe Edition (containing a bonus DVD) in 2011. The previous year's divorce between Björn and Agnetha was explored in "The Winner Takes It All", and the members' lives in Stockholm high society circles coloured the lyrics for "On and On and On". Other well-known songs on the album include the hit single title track "Super Trouper", as well as the electro-dance of "Lay All Your Love on Me". Probably due to the disco backlash at that time, the album saw ABBA returning to a more straightforward pop sound, as opposed to the preceding (and noticeably more dance-oriented) Voulez-Vous album. The album closed with "The Way Old Friends Do", which was recorded live a year earlier during their 1979 concert tour. wiki.content: Arrival is the fourth studio album by the Swedish pop group ABBA. It was originally released in Sweden on 11 October 1976 by Polar Records. Recording sessions began in August 1975 and continued until September 1976 at Metronome and Glen studios in Stockholm, Sweden. It became one of ABBA's most successful albums to date, producing three of their biggest hits: "Dancing Queen", "Money, Money, Money" and "Knowing Me, Knowing You". Upon its original 1976 release, "Fernando", released as a single earlier the same year, did not appear on Arrival, but it was included on the South African, Australian, and New Zealand versions. Arrival was the best-selling album of 1977 in the United Kingdom and was certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America. The album was first released on Compact disc in 1984 and then re-issued in digitally remastered form a total of four times; first in 1997, then in 2001, 2005 as part of The Complete Studio Recordings box set, and again in 2006 (as a special Deluxe Edition). wiki.content: ABBA is the third studio album by the Swedish pop group ABBA. It was originally released on 21 April 1975 through Polar Music and featured the hits "SOS", "I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do" and "Mamma Mia". Following the Eurovision success of "Waterloo", ABBA saw the band gaining worldwide recognition. "I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do" topped the charts in Australia, as did "Mamma Mia" shortly after. "SOS" and "Mamma Mia" became hits in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The album saw ABBA dabble with reggae on "Tropical Loveland" and includes a grand, pseudo-classical keyboard instrumental in the traditions of Keith Emerson and Rick Wakeman with "Intermezzo No. 1" (early working title: "Mama"). ABBA was first released on CD in Japan in 1986 by Polydor Records. This release contains a slightly different mix of "Man in the Middle" not found on any subsequent CD pressing and thus is highly sought after by collectors. ABBA was released on CD throughout Europe in 1987 also by Polydor, with five songs added from the Waterloo and Ring Ring albums, which were not available on CD until 1990. ABBA was released on CD in Sweden by Polar Music in 1988,[featuring the original 11 tracks only. The album has been reissued in digitally remastered form several times: in 1997 as part of "The ABBA Remasters" series with two bonus tracks, in 2001 with an updated cover artwork, in 2005 as part of The Complete Studio Recordings box set, and most recently in 2012 as a "Deluxe Edition". On the original UK cassette release of the album, "Bang-A-Boomerang" was split in two parts, being faded during the second verse at the end of side one and continued at the beginning of side two. wiki.content: Super Trouper is the seventh studio album by the Swedish pop group ABBA, released on 3 November 1980. It features the No.1 singles "The Winner Takes It All" and "Super Trouper". The album became the biggest-selling album of 1980 in the UK. Overview Led by the international hit "The Winner Takes It All", Super Trouper was the group's sixth chart-topping album in the UK. It was also the best-selling album in Britain for 1980. Super Trouper was first released on CD in 1983 by Polar Music International, in the early 1980s by Polydor, and in the late 1980s by Atlantic Records for the US. The album has been reissued in digitally remastered form four times; first in 1997, then in 2001, again in 2005 as part of The Complete Studio Recordings box set and as a Deluxe Edition (containing a bonus DVD) in 2011. The previous year's divorce between Björn and Agnetha was explored in "The Winner Takes It All", and the members' lives in Stockholm high society circles coloured the lyrics for "On and On and On". Other well-known songs on the album include the hit single title track "Super Trouper", as well as the electro-dance of "Lay All Your Love on Me". Probably due to the disco backlash at that time, the album saw ABBA returning to a more straightforward pop sound, as opposed to the preceding (and noticeably more dance-oriented) Voulez-Vous album. The album closed with "The Way Old Friends Do", which was recorded live a year earlier during their 1979 concert tour. wiki.content: Recording sessions for Waterloo began on 24 September 1973 with the track "Dance (While the Music Still Goes On)". This song was unusual in that it is the only ABBA track not to feature member Benny Andersson on keyboards, but instead featured American pianist John Rabbit Bundrick who was in Sweden at the time. Bundrick, however, was not credited on the album. Three weeks later the next two songs ("Suzy-Hang-Around" and "My Mama Said") went into the studio. A recording sheet from the day credits the artist as "ABBA", the first time the name was ever used in writing, the group until now being called "Björn & Benny, Agnetha & Anni-Frid", although their manager Stig Andersson had informally been calling them ABBA with the media for some time. The former of these songs marks the only time Benny Andersson sang lead on a track. 17 October saw the recording of two more tracks; "What About Livingstone" and "Honey Honey" - the latter being the second single released from the album in most countries. "King Kong Song" was recorded on 14 November, a song which members Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus today single out as one of their weakest tracks. This was also the date in which it was announced that ABBA were to appear at the Swedish selection for the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest. From that point, recording sessions speeded up and the rest of the tracks were recorded. Two songs were up for consideration for their Eurovision entry; "Waterloo" and "Hasta Mañana". The group preferred the former but felt the latter was a more safe bet. Ultimately they chose "Waterloo" as it was more the direction they wished to take the group. "Waterloo" and "Watch Out" were recorded on the same day - the songs that made up the lead single and its B-side. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: Arrival is the fourth studio album by the Swedish pop group ABBA. It was originally released in Sweden on 11 October 1976 by Polar Records. Recording sessions began in August 1975 and continued until September 1976 at Metronome and Glen studios in Stockholm, Sweden. It became one of ABBA's most successful albums to date, producing three of their biggest hits: "Dancing Queen", "Money, Money, Money" and "Knowing Me, Knowing You". Upon its original 1976 release, "Fernando", released as a single earlier the same year, did not appear on Arrival, but it was included on the South African, Australian, and New Zealand versions. Arrival was the best-selling album of 1977 in the United Kingdom and was certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America. The album was first released on Compact disc in 1984 and then re-issued in digitally remastered form a total of four times; first in 1997, then in 2001, 2005 as part of The Complete Studio Recordings box set, and again in 2006 (as a special Deluxe Edition). wiki.content: "The Lexicon of Love" is the debut studio album by English pop band ABC. It was released on 21 June 1982 by Neutron Records and reached number one on the UK Albums Chart, as well as the charts in New Zealand and Finland. The album was certified gold in the United States and platinum in the United Kingdom. Four of its singles, "Tears Are Not Enough", "Poison Arrow", "The Look of Love" and "All of My Heart", reached the UK top 20. Pitchfork ranked "All of My Heart" first on its "Now That's What I Call New Pop!" list. The album has frequently appeared in lists of the greatest albums of the 1980s. It was included in the 2018 edition of Robert Dimery's book "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die". ABC was formed by Stephen Singleton and Mark White under the name Vice Versa, initially as an electronic band. Martin Fry subsequently joined the group, which became ABC, with Fry as lead vocalist. The band's debut single, "Tears Are Not Enough", was released in 1981 and later remixed by producer Trevor Horn for inclusion on "The Lexicon of Love". The album's title originated from the headline of a review of an ABC concert published in NME. The band aimed to combine disco and post-punk influences. Fry cited the string arrangements of Chic and the musical style of Earth, Wind & Fire alongside the work of the Cure and Joy Division as influences on the album's sound. The group also sought to combine the sentimentality of mid-20th-century show tunes with contemporary songwriting. Although Fry admired synth-pop artists such as Gary Numan and Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, he wanted to focus on emotional and romantic themes rather than technology. All ten tracks concern romantic experiences, although Fry has denied that the album was intended as a concept album. The songs were written collectively by the band, with arranger and orchestrator Anne Dudley receiving additional songwriting credits on some tracks. Most of the album was recorded at Sarm East Studios in London, with further sessions taking place at Abbey Road, Townhouse, RAK and Good Earth studios. Horn produced the album, while Gary Langan served as engineer. J. J. Jeczalik programmed the Fairlight CMI, an early digital sampling instrument. Horn persuaded the band to replace bassist Mark Lickley with Brad Lang, whom he considered a more accomplished musician. In 1983, Horn, Langan, Dudley and Jeczalik formed the electronic music group Art of Noise. The production team and session musicians involved in "The Lexicon of Love" also contributed to the development of ZTT Records. The album's cover photograph was taken by Gered Mankowitz. Mercury Records handled its distribution in the United States and Japan, while Vertigo Records released it in Canada and Europe. "The Lexicon of Love" has been classified under several genres, including disco, pop, new wave, sophisti-pop, dance-pop, blue-eyed soul, synth-pop and lounge. It has also been associated with the new pop movement of the early 1980s. The singles "Tears Are Not Enough", "Poison Arrow", "The Look of Love" and "All of My Heart" all reached the UK top 20. "Poison Arrow" peaked at number 25 on the US charts, while "The Look of Love" reached number 18. The album reached number one in the United Kingdom and peaked at number 24 in the United States. It spent 50 weeks on the UK Albums Chart and was the country's fourth best-selling album of 1982. ABC toured Europe, the United States and Japan with an expanded line-up of session musicians, forming an 11-member ensemble. Concerts at the Hammersmith Odeon in London in November 1982 were recorded for the band's film "Mantrap", released in 1983. In 2004, Neutron Records issued a two-disc deluxe edition of "The Lexicon of Love" featuring previously unreleased outtakes, early demos and a live performance of the album recorded in 1982. In 2009, ABC performed the album in its entirety at the Royal Albert Hall in London, accompanied by the BBC Concert Orchestra and conducted by Dudley. Horn also appeared on stage. The album was performed in full again at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, on 18 December 2012 to mark its 30th anniversary. Dudley conducted the Southbank Sinfonia Orchestra for the performance. The ensemble subsequently completed a four-date mini-tour at the same venue on 30 March 2014. Between 4 and 9 November 2015, ABC and an orchestra performed the album at venues in Liverpool, Glasgow, Sheffield, London and Birmingham. A sequel, "The Lexicon of Love II", was released on 27 May 2016. In August 2023, a Blu-ray Audio edition featuring new Dolby Atmos and 5.1 surround sound remixes by Steven Wilson was released alongside a remastered vinyl edition of the original mix. The album received generally favourable reviews from critics. Publications and reference works including AllMusic, "Blender", "Christgau's Record Guide", "The Encyclopedia of Popular Music", "Mojo", "Q", "Rolling Stone", "The Rolling Stone Album Guide", "Select", "Spin Alternative Record Guide" and "The Great Rock Discography" awarded it positive ratings. Contemporary critic Mitchell Cohen of Creem described the album as a "piece of sumptuous kitsch", commenting on its elaborate arrangements, catchy melodies and resemblance to a collection of pop hits and advertising jingles. Robert Christgau awarded it an A−, praising Fry's lyrical wit and the album's synthetic funk rhythms while criticising aspects of his theatrical vocal delivery. Don Waller of the Los Angeles Times praised the songwriting, describing the tracks as expansive romantic compositions, but considered Fry's singing a weakness. Ken Tucker of The Philadelphia Inquirer offered a less favourable assessment, describing the album as dance music with limited emphasis on rhythm and excessive crooning. Retrospective reviews have generally praised the album's production and songwriting. AllMusic described Horn's production as dense and noisy but frequently beautiful, and noted that the emotional content of the songs gave the album a coherence that was absent from some of Horn's later productions. The review also highlighted tracks such as "Many Happy Returns" as examples of the band's combination of dance music and elaborate songwriting. In a BBC review of the 2004 deluxe edition, Rob Webb described "The Lexicon of Love" as a landmark in British pop music, praising ABC's wit, lyrics and funk influences. He characterised the songs as concise depictions of romantic relationships, ranging from the emotional themes of "All of My Heart" and "Show Me" to the bitterness of "Many Happy Returns". Colin Larkin awarded the album five stars in "The Encyclopedia of Popular Music", describing its pop songwriting as a benchmark for the genre during the 1980s and highlighting its collection of dramatic love songs. Reviewing a 2005 retrospective of Horn's work, Pitchfork also identified "The Lexicon of Love" as an essential album of its era. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: "The Razors Edge" is the twelfth studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC. It was released on 24 September 1990 through Albert Productions/CBS Records International in Australasia and Atlantic Records in Europe. The album was recorded in 1990 at Little Mountain Sound Studios in Vancouver, Canada. It was produced by Bruce Fairbairn, engineered and mixed by Mike Fraser, and mastered by George Marino at Sterling Sound in New York City. It was the only AC/DC studio album to feature Welsh drummer Chris Slade, who was a member of the band from 1989 to 1994. The album followed "Blow Up Your Video" (1988), which had been recorded with the band's original producers, Harry Vanda and George Young. After the subsequent tour began in 1988, rhythm guitarist Malcolm Young temporarily left touring activities to address issues related to alcoholism. He was replaced on tour by his nephew, Stevie Young. In 1989, drummer Simon Wright left the band to join the heavy metal group Dio and was replaced by Chris Slade. During this period, vocalist Brian Johnson was temporarily unavailable while finalising his divorce, leading Malcolm and Angus Young to write the material for the album themselves, a practice that continued on later AC/DC releases. Bruce Fairbairn, who had previously worked with bands including Aerosmith and Bon Jovi, was selected as producer for the album. According to the book "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", George Young was initially involved in the project but withdrew because of personal issues. The opening guitar riff of "Thunderstruck" was developed by Angus Young using a technique that alternated fretted notes with open strings. In interviews, Young stated that the riff originated from an improvised guitar idea that was later developed collaboratively with Malcolm Young over several months. The song became one of the album's best-known tracks. "Moneytalks" was also released as a single and became AC/DC's highest-charting single in the United States, reaching number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. During performances of the song on the accompanying tour, replica one-dollar bills known as "Angus Bucks" were dropped over audiences. A music video directed by David Mallet featured live footage from the tour. Several commentators noted lyrical themes related to wealth and business culture on tracks such as "Mistress for Christmas" and "Moneytalks". In a 1991 interview with "Guitar World", Angus Young described "Mistress for Christmas" as the album's funniest song and stated that the title track contained one of his preferred guitar solos from the record, including fingerpicking techniques that were uncommon in AC/DC's music. Upon release, "The Razors Edge" received mixed to positive reviews from music critics. Alex Henderson of AllMusic praised Brian Johnson's vocals and Angus Young's guitar work, while Greg Sandow of "Entertainment Weekly" gave the album a favourable assessment. Martin Popoff later described the album as an important comeback release for the band. In contrast, John Mendelsohn of "Rolling Stone" criticised the album for similarities to the band's earlier work. The album produced several singles, including "Thunderstruck", "Moneytalks", "Are You Ready", and "Rock Your Heart Out". "Thunderstruck" and "Are You Ready" reached numbers 5 and 16 respectively on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart. "Moneytalks" reached number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. "The Razors Edge" reached number 2 on the US Billboard 200 and remained on the chart for 77 consecutive weeks. It also reached number 4 on the UK Albums Chart. The album received multiple platinum certifications in several countries, including Canada, the United States, Australia, Germany, and Switzerland. Worldwide sales have been estimated at approximately 18.8 million copies, making it one of AC/DC's highest-selling albums. To promote the album, AC/DC embarked on the Razors Edge World Tour, which ran from November 1990 to November 1991. Performances from the tour were later used for the 1992 live album "AC/DC Live". "The Razors Edge" was reissued in 2003 as part of the "AC/DC Remasters" series and again in 2012 on iTunes alongside most of the band's catalogue. In 2024, it was reissued on gold vinyl as part of the "AC/DC 50" anniversary series. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: Highway to Hell is the sixth studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC, released in July 1979. It is also AC/DC's fifth international studio album. All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. It was the last album featuring Bon Scott, who died early the following year. The album has ten tracks: 1. "Highway to Hell" – 3:28 2. "Girls Got Rhythm" – 3:23 3. "Walk All Over You" – 5:10 4. "Touch Too Much" – 4:27 5. "Beating Around the Bush" – 3:56 6. "Shot Down in Flames" – 3:22 7. "Get It Hot" – 2:34 8. "If You Want Blood (You've Got It)" – 4:37 9. "Love Hungry Man" – 4:17 10. "Night Prowler" – 6:27 All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. It was originally released by Albert Productions, who licensed the album to Atlantic Records for release outside of Australia, and was then re-released by Epic Records in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. On May 25th 2006, Highway To Hell was certified 7x platinum by the RIAA. In 2003, the album was ranked number 199 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Overview Highway to Hell is the last AC/DC album recorded with lead vocalist Bon Scott before his death in February 1980. The final words spoken by Scott on the album are "Shazbot, na-nu na-nu," phrases used on the then-popular American sitcom, Mork and Mindy, by lead character Mork (a visiting extraterrestrial played by Robin Williams). Highway to Hell was the first AC/DC album not produced by Harry Vanda and George Young. Pre-production of the album began in January 1979 with demos cut at Albert Studios in Sydney, Australia, where they met the intended producer, Eddie Kramer. Kramer was fired before a single track had been completed, and Robert John "Mutt" Lange was brought in to replace him. The change proved to be fortuitous, with Lange also producing the band's biggest sellers, Back in Black and For Those About to Rock. The album was recorded during sessions in February 1979 at Criteria Studios in Miami, Florida and March-April at Roundhouse Studios in London, England. In Australia, Highway to Hell was released with a slightly different album cover, featuring flames and a drawing of a bass guitar neck superimposed over the same group photo used on the international cover. Additionally, the East German release had different and much plainer designs on the front and back, apparently because the authorities were not happy with the sleeve as released elsewhere. wiki.content: "Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released on 25 July 1980 by Albert Productions and Atlantic Records. It is the band's first album with Brian Johnson as lead vocalist, following the death of previous singer Bon Scott earlier in 1980. After the commercial success of the 1979 album "Highway to Hell", the band had planned to continue recording material for a follow-up. In February 1980, Bon Scott died in London after a night of heavy drinking. The cause of death was recorded as acute alcohol poisoning and classified as death by misadventure. The group briefly considered disbanding but ultimately decided to continue and recruited Brian Johnson, formerly of the band Geordie, as their new singer. The album was written by Johnson and brothers Angus and Malcolm Young, and produced by Robert John "Mutt" Lange, who had also worked on "Highway to Hell". Recording took place over approximately seven weeks between April and May 1980 at Compass Point Studios in Nassau, Bahamas. The sessions were later mixed at Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The band has stated that the album's all-black cover was intended as a gesture of mourning for Bon Scott, although the record label initially expressed reservations about the design. Prior to joining AC/DC, Brian Johnson was selected after auditions held following Scott's death. He impressed the band during rehearsals and was officially offered the position in March 1980. During the transition period, the band focused on preparing new material, some of which developed from earlier ideas. The recording process was influenced by challenging environmental conditions in the Bahamas, including storms and power disruptions. Johnson has described the sessions as demanding, particularly due to producer Mutt Lange's emphasis on precise vocal performances. Engineer Tony Platt also noted that adapting the studio environment to the band's sound presented difficulties. Several elements contributed to the album's production, including the use of a Schaffer–Vega wireless system to achieve a distinctive guitar sound. A bell sound featured on the opening track "Hells Bells" was ultimately recorded using a custom-made bell after alternative recordings were considered insufficient. The album's title track and other songs reflect themes typical of the band's established style, including high-energy rock arrangements and straightforward lyrical structures. "Back in Black" was released first in the United States in July 1980, followed by releases in Europe and Australia in August of the same year. It achieved immediate commercial success, reaching high chart positions in several countries, including number one in the United Kingdom and number four in the United States. The album remained in the US Top 10 for several months and contributed to renewed interest in the band's earlier catalogue, with previous albums re-entering charts in the UK. In the United States, the earlier album "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap" was also reissued following the success of "Back in Black" and later achieved a higher chart position than the album itself. Music videos were produced for several tracks, including "You Shook Me All Night Long", "Hells Bells", "Back in Black", and "Rock and Roll Ain't Noise Pollution". "You Shook Me All Night Long" became the band's first single to enter the US Top 40, peaking at number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album was supported by a long international tour, which contributed to the band's growing global profile in the early 1980s. Commercially, "Back in Black" became one of the best-selling albums in music history, with estimates of around 50 million copies sold worldwide. In the United States, it has been certified multiple times platinum and is among the highest-selling albums in that market. In 2024 it was certified 27× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, reflecting 27 million units sold in the US. It is also widely cited as one of the best-selling rock albums ever released and one of the most commercially successful albums not to reach number one on the US charts. Critical reception of the album has been mixed but generally positive in retrospective assessments. Some reviewers have described it as a defining hard rock record characterised by its direct production style and consistent songwriting, while others have criticised aspects of its lyrical content and thematic focus. Early reviews varied, with some praising its energy and cohesion and others finding the material repetitive. Retrospective commentary has often emphasised its influence and durability within rock music, while also noting that certain lyrical themes reflect the attitudes of its time. The album has frequently appeared on "greatest albums" lists published by music magazines and organisations. It has been included in rankings such as Rolling Stone's lists of greatest albums of all time in multiple editions, VH1's album rankings, and Time magazine's list of influential albums. The title track has also been widely recognised in lists of notable rock songs. Over time, "Back in Black" has been regarded as a landmark release in AC/DC's career and a major commercial success in rock music history. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: High Voltage is the first internationally released album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC. It contains tracks from their first two Australia-only issued albums, High Voltage and T.N.T. (both from 1975). Originally released on Atlantic Records, this edition of High Voltage has proven popular, selling three million units in the US alone. However, initially the album was panned by some critics upon its release, including a review by Rolling Stone magazine's Billy Altman that called it an "all-time low" for the hard rock genre. It was re-released in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Tracklist Side A 1 It's A Long Way To The Top (If You Wanna Rock 'N' Roll) 2 Rock 'N' Roll Singer 3 The Jack 4 Live Wire 5 T.N.T. wiki.content: Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap is the second international studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC, released in December 1976 in Europe and delayed for release in the U.S. until April 1981. All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. Originally released on Atlantic Records, it peaked at #3 and is currently certified 6x platinum by the RIAA. The album was re-released in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Overview This edition of Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap is considerably different from the original Australian edition released in September 1976, featuring a different cover and track order. On this album, the Australian version's "R.I.P. (Rock in Peace)" and "Jailbreak" are replaced by "Rocker" (from 1975's T.N.T.) and "Love at First Feel", the latter being one of only two tracks from international AC/DC albums not available on the band's Australian albums. (The other is "Cold Hearted Man", released on European pressings of Powerage.) Conversely, several songs that are available on Australian AC/DC albums have not seen overseas release. However, "Love at First Feel" was released in Australia as a single. Though the international album was released by Atlantic Records in Europe in 1976 it was not picked up for U.S. release at the time. Following the American success of Highway To Hell in late 1979 import copies of the album, began to appear as imports in the U.S. Some of these imports were the original Australian edition on Albert Productions. However Atlantic Records also pressed the international version in Australia and many of these copies were also exported to the U.S. Strong demand for both import versions eventually led the U.S. division of Atlantic to finally authorize an official U.S. release in April 1981 which went straight to #3 on the Billboard album charts. Two songs on the international album were edited from the full length versions on the original Australian album. The full length "Dirty Deeds" has the title of the song chanted 4 times starting at 3:09, but on the edited version the chant is heard only 2 times. "Ain't No Fun" lasted 7:29 on the Australian album but was faded out early to 6:57 on the international version. However, both these full length versions were restored on the 1994 Atco Records remastered CD of the international album. The most recent 2003 CD edition on Epic Records goes back to the edited versions as on the 1976 and 1981 international vinyl editions. Additionally, a song titled "I'm a Rebel" was recorded during the Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap sessions in September 1976, with music and lyrics written by Angus and Malcolm Young's older brother, Alex Young. This song was never released and remains in Albert Productions' vaults. Angus came up with the title of the album when he was watching an episode of Beany And Cecil. The antagonist, Dishonest John, carried a card that read: "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap, Special Holidays, Sundays and Rates". The 1994 remastered CD on Atco Records contains full length versions of both songs. The track "Rocker" was originally released on T.N.T. in 1975. wiki.content: "Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released on 25 July 1980 by Albert Productions and Atlantic Records. It is the band's first album with Brian Johnson as lead vocalist, following the death of previous singer Bon Scott earlier in 1980. After the commercial success of the 1979 album "Highway to Hell", the band had planned to continue recording material for a follow-up. In February 1980, Bon Scott died in London after a night of heavy drinking. The cause of death was recorded as acute alcohol poisoning and classified as death by misadventure. The group briefly considered disbanding but ultimately decided to continue and recruited Brian Johnson, formerly of the band Geordie, as their new singer. The album was written by Johnson and brothers Angus and Malcolm Young, and produced by Robert John "Mutt" Lange, who had also worked on "Highway to Hell". Recording took place over approximately seven weeks between April and May 1980 at Compass Point Studios in Nassau, Bahamas. The sessions were later mixed at Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The band has stated that the album's all-black cover was intended as a gesture of mourning for Bon Scott, although the record label initially expressed reservations about the design. Prior to joining AC/DC, Brian Johnson was selected after auditions held following Scott's death. He impressed the band during rehearsals and was officially offered the position in March 1980. During the transition period, the band focused on preparing new material, some of which developed from earlier ideas. The recording process was influenced by challenging environmental conditions in the Bahamas, including storms and power disruptions. Johnson has described the sessions as demanding, particularly due to producer Mutt Lange's emphasis on precise vocal performances. Engineer Tony Platt also noted that adapting the studio environment to the band's sound presented difficulties. Several elements contributed to the album's production, including the use of a Schaffer–Vega wireless system to achieve a distinctive guitar sound. A bell sound featured on the opening track "Hells Bells" was ultimately recorded using a custom-made bell after alternative recordings were considered insufficient. The album's title track and other songs reflect themes typical of the band's established style, including high-energy rock arrangements and straightforward lyrical structures. "Back in Black" was released first in the United States in July 1980, followed by releases in Europe and Australia in August of the same year. It achieved immediate commercial success, reaching high chart positions in several countries, including number one in the United Kingdom and number four in the United States. The album remained in the US Top 10 for several months and contributed to renewed interest in the band's earlier catalogue, with previous albums re-entering charts in the UK. In the United States, the earlier album "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap" was also reissued following the success of "Back in Black" and later achieved a higher chart position than the album itself. Music videos were produced for several tracks, including "You Shook Me All Night Long", "Hells Bells", "Back in Black", and "Rock and Roll Ain't Noise Pollution". "You Shook Me All Night Long" became the band's first single to enter the US Top 40, peaking at number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album was supported by a long international tour, which contributed to the band's growing global profile in the early 1980s. Commercially, "Back in Black" became one of the best-selling albums in music history, with estimates of around 50 million copies sold worldwide. In the United States, it has been certified multiple times platinum and is among the highest-selling albums in that market. In 2024 it was certified 27× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, reflecting 27 million units sold in the US. It is also widely cited as one of the best-selling rock albums ever released and one of the most commercially successful albums not to reach number one on the US charts. Critical reception of the album has been mixed but generally positive in retrospective assessments. Some reviewers have described it as a defining hard rock record characterised by its direct production style and consistent songwriting, while others have criticised aspects of its lyrical content and thematic focus. Early reviews varied, with some praising its energy and cohesion and others finding the material repetitive. Retrospective commentary has often emphasised its influence and durability within rock music, while also noting that certain lyrical themes reflect the attitudes of its time. The album has frequently appeared on "greatest albums" lists published by music magazines and organisations. It has been included in rankings such as Rolling Stone's lists of greatest albums of all time in multiple editions, VH1's album rankings, and Time magazine's list of influential albums. The title track has also been widely recognised in lists of notable rock songs. Over time, "Back in Black" has been regarded as a landmark release in AC/DC's career and a major commercial success in rock music history. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: "The Razors Edge" is the twelfth studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC. It was released on 24 September 1990 through Albert Productions/CBS Records International in Australasia and Atlantic Records in Europe. The album was recorded in 1990 at Little Mountain Sound Studios in Vancouver, Canada. It was produced by Bruce Fairbairn, engineered and mixed by Mike Fraser, and mastered by George Marino at Sterling Sound in New York City. It was the only AC/DC studio album to feature Welsh drummer Chris Slade, who was a member of the band from 1989 to 1994. The album followed "Blow Up Your Video" (1988), which had been recorded with the band's original producers, Harry Vanda and George Young. After the subsequent tour began in 1988, rhythm guitarist Malcolm Young temporarily left touring activities to address issues related to alcoholism. He was replaced on tour by his nephew, Stevie Young. In 1989, drummer Simon Wright left the band to join the heavy metal group Dio and was replaced by Chris Slade. During this period, vocalist Brian Johnson was temporarily unavailable while finalising his divorce, leading Malcolm and Angus Young to write the material for the album themselves, a practice that continued on later AC/DC releases. Bruce Fairbairn, who had previously worked with bands including Aerosmith and Bon Jovi, was selected as producer for the album. According to the book "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", George Young was initially involved in the project but withdrew because of personal issues. The opening guitar riff of "Thunderstruck" was developed by Angus Young using a technique that alternated fretted notes with open strings. In interviews, Young stated that the riff originated from an improvised guitar idea that was later developed collaboratively with Malcolm Young over several months. The song became one of the album's best-known tracks. "Moneytalks" was also released as a single and became AC/DC's highest-charting single in the United States, reaching number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. During performances of the song on the accompanying tour, replica one-dollar bills known as "Angus Bucks" were dropped over audiences. A music video directed by David Mallet featured live footage from the tour. Several commentators noted lyrical themes related to wealth and business culture on tracks such as "Mistress for Christmas" and "Moneytalks". In a 1991 interview with "Guitar World", Angus Young described "Mistress for Christmas" as the album's funniest song and stated that the title track contained one of his preferred guitar solos from the record, including fingerpicking techniques that were uncommon in AC/DC's music. Upon release, "The Razors Edge" received mixed to positive reviews from music critics. Alex Henderson of AllMusic praised Brian Johnson's vocals and Angus Young's guitar work, while Greg Sandow of "Entertainment Weekly" gave the album a favourable assessment. Martin Popoff later described the album as an important comeback release for the band. In contrast, John Mendelsohn of "Rolling Stone" criticised the album for similarities to the band's earlier work. The album produced several singles, including "Thunderstruck", "Moneytalks", "Are You Ready", and "Rock Your Heart Out". "Thunderstruck" and "Are You Ready" reached numbers 5 and 16 respectively on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart. "Moneytalks" reached number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. "The Razors Edge" reached number 2 on the US Billboard 200 and remained on the chart for 77 consecutive weeks. It also reached number 4 on the UK Albums Chart. The album received multiple platinum certifications in several countries, including Canada, the United States, Australia, Germany, and Switzerland. Worldwide sales have been estimated at approximately 18.8 million copies, making it one of AC/DC's highest-selling albums. To promote the album, AC/DC embarked on the Razors Edge World Tour, which ran from November 1990 to November 1991. Performances from the tour were later used for the 1992 live album "AC/DC Live". "The Razors Edge" was reissued in 2003 as part of the "AC/DC Remasters" series and again in 2012 on iTunes alongside most of the band's catalogue. In 2024, it was reissued on gold vinyl as part of the "AC/DC 50" anniversary series. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: "For Those About to Rock (We Salute You)" (shortened to "For Those About to Rock" on the album cover) is the eighth studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC. It was released on 20 November 1981 in the United States and on 27 November 1981 in the United Kingdom. The album followed AC/DC's 1980 release "Back in Black". It sold more than four million copies in the United States and became the band's first number-one album on the Billboard chart. It remained AC/DC's only number-one album in the United States until the release of "Black Ice" in 2008. In Australia, the album reached number three on the Kent Music Report Albums Chart. Recorded in Paris, the album marked the third and final collaboration between AC/DC and producer Robert John "Mutt" Lange. It was reissued in 2003 as part of the "AC/DC Remasters" series. Following the "Back in Black Tour", the band took a short break before returning to Paris in June 1981 for rehearsals. Most of the material for the album had reportedly been written by that time. Recording sessions began on 6 July 1981 at EMI's Pathé Marconi Studios in Paris, with Lange producing. After approximately ten days, the sessions were abandoned because Lange was dissatisfied with the recorded sound. After searching for another studio, the band resumed recording later in July at H.I.S. Studio, a rehearsal space in Paris, using the Mobile One recording truck from London. The recording process was further interrupted when the band performed at the Monsters of Rock festival at Castle Donington on 22 August 1981. The performance was reportedly affected by poor weather conditions and limited preparation time. During the sessions, tensions also developed over Lange's detailed production methods, and the band ended its working relationship with him after the album's completion. "For Those About to Rock (We Salute You)" topped the Billboard album chart in the United States for three weeks and achieved sales of approximately four million copies there. The album's singles, "Let's Get It Up" and "For Those About to Rock (We Salute You)", reached numbers 13 and 15 respectively on the UK Singles Chart. Worldwide sales have been estimated at around seven million copies. Critical reception was mixed to positive. Rolling Stone described the album favorably in its original 1981 review. In a later review, David Fricke praised the title track's "unusual stop-start effect". Music critic Robert Christgau commented on Brian Johnson's vocal style and the album's lyrical content in a more critical assessment. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: Let There Be Rock is the third international studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC, released in June 1977. All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. Originally released on Atlantic Records, this edition has sold over 2 million copies in the United States. The album was re-released in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Overview Let There Be Rock is the last AC/DC recording to feature bassist Mark Evans, who previously played on the international versions of High Voltage (May 1976) and Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap (December 1976). As with AC/DC's previous albums, there were differences between the international and Australian edition of Let There Be Rock, released in March 1977. For the US market (and later for the CD releases), the Australian version's racy "Crabsody In Blue" was replaced with a shortened version of "Problem Child" from AC/DC's Dirty Deeds Done Cheap, released in September 1976. The international version also has a slightly modified track order. Additionally, the international version of Let There Be Rock featured a different cover from that of the original. This cover marked the debut of AC/DC's classic logo. The Australian edition was eventually repackaged with the international version's cover, marking the first time an Australian AC/DC album cover was matched to its corresponding international edition. In 1980, AC/DC released a live concert motion picture entitled AC/DC: Let There Be Rock. In 1997, an expanded audio recording of this concert was released on CD as Let There Be Rock: The Movie, on discs 2-3 of the Bonfire box set. The title track, "Let There Be Rock" will mark the band's music video game debut when it is featured in the upcoming rhythm game Rock Band 2. Most CD releases feature this track listing along with a slightly longer version of "Go Down". Track 5 ("Problem Child") originally released on Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap in 1976. This is a shortened version of the original. For the original vinyl release, in all markets other than the USA and Japan, "Crabsody In Blue" was featured instead of "Problem Child". wiki.content: "Who Made Who" is a soundtrack album by the Australian hard rock band AC/DC. It was released on 26 May 1986 as the soundtrack for the Stephen King film "Maximum Overdrive". The album was reissued in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Three tracks on the album – "Who Made Who", "D.T." and "Chase the Ace" – were newly written and recorded specifically for the release. The remaining tracks were previously issued by the band on earlier albums. Only the song "Ride On" features former lead vocalist Bon Scott, who died in 1980, while the other tracks feature his successor Brian Johnson. In conjunction with the album, AC/DC released a 24-minute video compilation containing promotional videos for "Who Made Who", "You Shook Me All Night Long", a remixed version of "Shake Your Foundations", and "Hells Bells", as well as live footage of "For Those About to Rock (We Salute You)" recorded in Detroit in 1983. The music video for the title track, directed by David Mallet, was filmed at the Brixton Academy in London. It features numerous performers portraying clones of guitarist Angus Young. According to "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", the participants included several hundred fans, many of whom waited overnight outside the venue to take part, including members of the band's UK fan club and individuals who had learned of the event through radio announcements. "Who Made Who" was written for "Maximum Overdrive", a film in which machines become autonomous and hostile toward humans. The song's lyrics address themes related to technology created by humans gaining control over their creators and the resulting reversal of power dynamics. Although "Maximum Overdrive" received negative critical reception and performed poorly at the box office, the soundtrack achieved commercial success. It reached number 16 on the UK Albums Chart and number 33 on the US Billboard 200. The title track became one of the band's most successful singles in several years, reaching the top 10 in Australia and number 16 in the United Kingdom. It was also voted the second-best track of 1986 by readers of Hit Parader magazine. A re-release of "You Shook Me All Night Long" from the album reached number 46 in the UK singles chart. The album has sold approximately five million copies in the United States. Reviewer Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic described the album as a retrospective of AC/DC's work and noted the inclusion of selected tracks from earlier, less successful albums. wiki.content: "The Razors Edge" is the twelfth studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC. It was released on 24 September 1990 through Albert Productions/CBS Records International in Australasia and Atlantic Records in Europe. The album was recorded in 1990 at Little Mountain Sound Studios in Vancouver, Canada. It was produced by Bruce Fairbairn, engineered and mixed by Mike Fraser, and mastered by George Marino at Sterling Sound in New York City. It was the only AC/DC studio album to feature Welsh drummer Chris Slade, who was a member of the band from 1989 to 1994. The album followed "Blow Up Your Video" (1988), which had been recorded with the band's original producers, Harry Vanda and George Young. After the subsequent tour began in 1988, rhythm guitarist Malcolm Young temporarily left touring activities to address issues related to alcoholism. He was replaced on tour by his nephew, Stevie Young. In 1989, drummer Simon Wright left the band to join the heavy metal group Dio and was replaced by Chris Slade. During this period, vocalist Brian Johnson was temporarily unavailable while finalising his divorce, leading Malcolm and Angus Young to write the material for the album themselves, a practice that continued on later AC/DC releases. Bruce Fairbairn, who had previously worked with bands including Aerosmith and Bon Jovi, was selected as producer for the album. According to the book "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", George Young was initially involved in the project but withdrew because of personal issues. The opening guitar riff of "Thunderstruck" was developed by Angus Young using a technique that alternated fretted notes with open strings. In interviews, Young stated that the riff originated from an improvised guitar idea that was later developed collaboratively with Malcolm Young over several months. The song became one of the album's best-known tracks. "Moneytalks" was also released as a single and became AC/DC's highest-charting single in the United States, reaching number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. During performances of the song on the accompanying tour, replica one-dollar bills known as "Angus Bucks" were dropped over audiences. A music video directed by David Mallet featured live footage from the tour. Several commentators noted lyrical themes related to wealth and business culture on tracks such as "Mistress for Christmas" and "Moneytalks". In a 1991 interview with "Guitar World", Angus Young described "Mistress for Christmas" as the album's funniest song and stated that the title track contained one of his preferred guitar solos from the record, including fingerpicking techniques that were uncommon in AC/DC's music. Upon release, "The Razors Edge" received mixed to positive reviews from music critics. Alex Henderson of AllMusic praised Brian Johnson's vocals and Angus Young's guitar work, while Greg Sandow of "Entertainment Weekly" gave the album a favourable assessment. Martin Popoff later described the album as an important comeback release for the band. In contrast, John Mendelsohn of "Rolling Stone" criticised the album for similarities to the band's earlier work. The album produced several singles, including "Thunderstruck", "Moneytalks", "Are You Ready", and "Rock Your Heart Out". "Thunderstruck" and "Are You Ready" reached numbers 5 and 16 respectively on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart. "Moneytalks" reached number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100. "The Razors Edge" reached number 2 on the US Billboard 200 and remained on the chart for 77 consecutive weeks. It also reached number 4 on the UK Albums Chart. The album received multiple platinum certifications in several countries, including Canada, the United States, Australia, Germany, and Switzerland. Worldwide sales have been estimated at approximately 18.8 million copies, making it one of AC/DC's highest-selling albums. To promote the album, AC/DC embarked on the Razors Edge World Tour, which ran from November 1990 to November 1991. Performances from the tour were later used for the 1992 live album "AC/DC Live". "The Razors Edge" was reissued in 2003 as part of the "AC/DC Remasters" series and again in 2012 on iTunes alongside most of the band's catalogue. In 2024, it was reissued on gold vinyl as part of the "AC/DC 50" anniversary series. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: "Rock or Bust" is the sixteenth studio album by the Australian rock band AC/DC, released on 28 November 2014 in Australia and New Zealand and on 2 December 2014 in other territories. It is the band's first album to feature rhythm guitarist Stevie Young, who replaced founding member Malcolm Young after his retirement due to health issues. Malcolm Young later died in 2017. At approximately 35 minutes in length, the album became AC/DC's shortest studio album, surpassing 1983's "Flick of the Switch". It was also the band's first album of original material since 2008's "Black Ice". Worldwide sales reached approximately 2.8 million copies. The album was recorded at Warehouse Studio in Vancouver, Canada, with producer Brendan O'Brien and mixer Mike Fraser. According to Angus Young, the recording process lasted around four weeks. Much of the material was developed from song ideas accumulated by Angus and Malcolm Young during earlier recording sessions. Although Malcolm Young received songwriting credits on all tracks, his guitar parts were performed by Stevie Young. Prior to the album's announcement, lead vocalist Brian Johnson stated that recording without Malcolm Young had been challenging. He noted that the working title "Man Down" had been considered but was ultimately rejected. The album's artwork was directed by Josh Cheuse of Arcade Creative Group. The physical edition featured a lenticular cover and a booklet containing 24 photographs of the band. Promotional activities included a video campaign created in a Polish quarry, where an AC/DC logo was revealed through a controlled rock explosion. The lead single, "Play Ball", was first used in a trailer for Major League Baseball postseason coverage on TBS in September 2014 and was released as a single on 7 October 2014. The album's track listing and artwork were revealed on the same day. A second single, "Rock or Bust", was released on 17 November 2014. Its music video was filmed in London before an audience of 500 fans. During the filming of both videos, drummer Phil Rudd was absent and was replaced by Welsh drummer Bob Richards. On 6 November 2014, Phil Rudd was arrested in New Zealand on charges that initially included attempting to procure the murder of two men. The most serious charge was dropped the following day, while charges relating to drug possession and threatening to kill remained. AC/DC stated that the legal proceedings would not affect the album's release or the planned tour. "Rock or Bust" achieved commercial success internationally. It reached number one in twelve countries, including Australia, Canada, Germany and Sweden, and entered the top five in a further twelve countries, including New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy. The single "Play Ball" reached the top 40 in several countries, including Spain, France and Switzerland. In the United States, the album debuted at number three on the Billboard 200, selling 172,000 copies in its first week. By January 2015, sales in the country had reached 500,000 copies, earning a gold certification from the Recording Industry Association of America. In Canada, the album debuted at number one on the Canadian Albums Chart with first-week sales of 31,000 copies. Critical reception was generally favourable. Review aggregation website Metacritic assigned the album a score of 75 out of 100 based on 22 reviews, indicating generally positive reviews. Critics frequently noted the album's adherence to AC/DC's established hard rock style, with particular attention given to its guitar riffs, choruses and concise running time. To promote the album, AC/DC embarked on the "Rock or Bust World Tour" in 2015, which also marked the band's 40th anniversary. Stevie Young performed Malcolm Young's role on the tour. Chris Slade, who had previously been a member of the band between 1989 and 1994, replaced Phil Rudd on drums. Four songs from the album were regularly performed live: "Rock or Bust", "Play Ball", "Got Some Rock & Roll Thunder" and "Baptism by Fire". During the tour, lead vocalist Brian Johnson withdrew from performing due to hearing problems and was replaced for the 2016 dates by Axl Rose of Guns N' Roses. Following the conclusion of the tour, bassist Cliff Williams retired from the band. Johnson, Williams and Rudd subsequently returned to AC/DC. The album received several award nominations and honours. In 2015, it won the Planet Rock Award for Best International Album. It also received ECHO Award nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rock/Alternative International Group, winning the latter category. At the 2015 ARIA Music Awards, AC/DC were nominated for Best Group but lost to Tame Impala. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: Let There Be Rock is the third international studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC, released in June 1977. All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. Originally released on Atlantic Records, this edition has sold over 2 million copies in the United States. The album was re-released in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Overview Let There Be Rock is the last AC/DC recording to feature bassist Mark Evans, who previously played on the international versions of High Voltage (May 1976) and Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap (December 1976). As with AC/DC's previous albums, there were differences between the international and Australian edition of Let There Be Rock, released in March 1977. For the US market (and later for the CD releases), the Australian version's racy "Crabsody In Blue" was replaced with a shortened version of "Problem Child" from AC/DC's Dirty Deeds Done Cheap, released in September 1976. The international version also has a slightly modified track order. Additionally, the international version of Let There Be Rock featured a different cover from that of the original. This cover marked the debut of AC/DC's classic logo. The Australian edition was eventually repackaged with the international version's cover, marking the first time an Australian AC/DC album cover was matched to its corresponding international edition. In 1980, AC/DC released a live concert motion picture entitled AC/DC: Let There Be Rock. In 1997, an expanded audio recording of this concert was released on CD as Let There Be Rock: The Movie, on discs 2-3 of the Bonfire box set. The title track, "Let There Be Rock" will mark the band's music video game debut when it is featured in the upcoming rhythm game Rock Band 2. Most CD releases feature this track listing along with a slightly longer version of "Go Down". Track 5 ("Problem Child") originally released on Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap in 1976. This is a shortened version of the original. For the original vinyl release, in all markets other than the USA and Japan, "Crabsody In Blue" was featured instead of "Problem Child". wiki.content: Highway to Hell is the sixth studio album by Australian hard rock band AC/DC, released in July 1979. It is also AC/DC's fifth international studio album. All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. It was the last album featuring Bon Scott, who died early the following year. The album has ten tracks: 1. "Highway to Hell" – 3:28 2. "Girls Got Rhythm" – 3:23 3. "Walk All Over You" – 5:10 4. "Touch Too Much" – 4:27 5. "Beating Around the Bush" – 3:56 6. "Shot Down in Flames" – 3:22 7. "Get It Hot" – 2:34 8. "If You Want Blood (You've Got It)" – 4:37 9. "Love Hungry Man" – 4:17 10. "Night Prowler" – 6:27 All songs were written by Angus Young, Malcolm Young, and Bon Scott. It was originally released by Albert Productions, who licensed the album to Atlantic Records for release outside of Australia, and was then re-released by Epic Records in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. On May 25th 2006, Highway To Hell was certified 7x platinum by the RIAA. In 2003, the album was ranked number 199 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Overview Highway to Hell is the last AC/DC album recorded with lead vocalist Bon Scott before his death in February 1980. The final words spoken by Scott on the album are "Shazbot, na-nu na-nu," phrases used on the then-popular American sitcom, Mork and Mindy, by lead character Mork (a visiting extraterrestrial played by Robin Williams). Highway to Hell was the first AC/DC album not produced by Harry Vanda and George Young. Pre-production of the album began in January 1979 with demos cut at Albert Studios in Sydney, Australia, where they met the intended producer, Eddie Kramer. Kramer was fired before a single track had been completed, and Robert John "Mutt" Lange was brought in to replace him. The change proved to be fortuitous, with Lange also producing the band's biggest sellers, Back in Black and For Those About to Rock. The album was recorded during sessions in February 1979 at Criteria Studios in Miami, Florida and March-April at Roundhouse Studios in London, England. In Australia, Highway to Hell was released with a slightly different album cover, featuring flames and a drawing of a bass guitar neck superimposed over the same group photo used on the international cover. Additionally, the East German release had different and much plainer designs on the front and back, apparently because the authorities were not happy with the sleeve as released elsewhere. wiki.content: "Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released on 25 July 1980 by Albert Productions and Atlantic Records. It is the band's first album with Brian Johnson as lead vocalist, following the death of previous singer Bon Scott earlier in 1980. After the commercial success of the 1979 album "Highway to Hell", the band had planned to continue recording material for a follow-up. In February 1980, Bon Scott died in London after a night of heavy drinking. The cause of death was recorded as acute alcohol poisoning and classified as death by misadventure. The group briefly considered disbanding but ultimately decided to continue and recruited Brian Johnson, formerly of the band Geordie, as their new singer. The album was written by Johnson and brothers Angus and Malcolm Young, and produced by Robert John "Mutt" Lange, who had also worked on "Highway to Hell". Recording took place over approximately seven weeks between April and May 1980 at Compass Point Studios in Nassau, Bahamas. The sessions were later mixed at Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The band has stated that the album's all-black cover was intended as a gesture of mourning for Bon Scott, although the record label initially expressed reservations about the design. Prior to joining AC/DC, Brian Johnson was selected after auditions held following Scott's death. He impressed the band during rehearsals and was officially offered the position in March 1980. During the transition period, the band focused on preparing new material, some of which developed from earlier ideas. The recording process was influenced by challenging environmental conditions in the Bahamas, including storms and power disruptions. Johnson has described the sessions as demanding, particularly due to producer Mutt Lange's emphasis on precise vocal performances. Engineer Tony Platt also noted that adapting the studio environment to the band's sound presented difficulties. Several elements contributed to the album's production, including the use of a Schaffer–Vega wireless system to achieve a distinctive guitar sound. A bell sound featured on the opening track "Hells Bells" was ultimately recorded using a custom-made bell after alternative recordings were considered insufficient. The album's title track and other songs reflect themes typical of the band's established style, including high-energy rock arrangements and straightforward lyrical structures. "Back in Black" was released first in the United States in July 1980, followed by releases in Europe and Australia in August of the same year. It achieved immediate commercial success, reaching high chart positions in several countries, including number one in the United Kingdom and number four in the United States. The album remained in the US Top 10 for several months and contributed to renewed interest in the band's earlier catalogue, with previous albums re-entering charts in the UK. In the United States, the earlier album "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap" was also reissued following the success of "Back in Black" and later achieved a higher chart position than the album itself. Music videos were produced for several tracks, including "You Shook Me All Night Long", "Hells Bells", "Back in Black", and "Rock and Roll Ain't Noise Pollution". "You Shook Me All Night Long" became the band's first single to enter the US Top 40, peaking at number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album was supported by a long international tour, which contributed to the band's growing global profile in the early 1980s. Commercially, "Back in Black" became one of the best-selling albums in music history, with estimates of around 50 million copies sold worldwide. In the United States, it has been certified multiple times platinum and is among the highest-selling albums in that market. In 2024 it was certified 27× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, reflecting 27 million units sold in the US. It is also widely cited as one of the best-selling rock albums ever released and one of the most commercially successful albums not to reach number one on the US charts. Critical reception of the album has been mixed but generally positive in retrospective assessments. Some reviewers have described it as a defining hard rock record characterised by its direct production style and consistent songwriting, while others have criticised aspects of its lyrical content and thematic focus. Early reviews varied, with some praising its energy and cohesion and others finding the material repetitive. Retrospective commentary has often emphasised its influence and durability within rock music, while also noting that certain lyrical themes reflect the attitudes of its time. The album has frequently appeared on "greatest albums" lists published by music magazines and organisations. It has been included in rankings such as Rolling Stone's lists of greatest albums of all time in multiple editions, VH1's album rankings, and Time magazine's list of influential albums. The title track has also been widely recognised in lists of notable rock songs. wiki.content: "Stiff Upper Lip" is the fourteenth studio album by the Australian hard rock band AC/DC. It was released on 28 February 2000. The album was produced by George Young, older brother of Malcolm and Angus Young. It was the last AC/DC album he produced before his death in 2017. The album was re-released in the United States in 2007 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series and in the United Kingdom in 2005. The Young brothers began writing material for what would become "Stiff Upper Lip" in the summer of 1997 in London and the Netherlands, with Malcolm Young on guitar and Angus Young on drums. By February 1998, the songs had been completed. The band had reportedly intended to record the album with Canadian producer Bruce Fairbairn, who had previously worked with AC/DC on "The Razors Edge" and "AC/DC Live", but he died in May 1999 before the project could proceed. The band instead worked with George Young and Mike Fraser, who had previously co-produced "Ballbreaker" with Rick Rubin, to complete the album. Recording and mixing took place at Bryan Adams' Warehouse Studios in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, between September and November 1999. Eighteen songs were recorded during the sessions. Bassist Cliff Williams later described the album in an interview for VH1's "Behind the Music" as an easy recording process due to the material being largely prepared in advance. According to Arnaud Durieux's memoir "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", Malcolm Young plays a guitar solo on "Can't Stand Still", while Angus Young contributes backing vocals on "Hold Me Back". The album is often described in secondary sources as drawing on blues influences more strongly than its predecessor "Ballbreaker". Brian Johnson commented in an interview with Guitar World that George Young's production approach was more direct and organised than previous collaborative production setups, and that the band worked long hours during recording sessions. Angus Young stated in interviews that the album title came to him while he was in traffic, and was inspired by the idea of lips as a recurring symbol in rock and roll, referencing performers such as Elvis Presley and Mick Jagger. He also discussed the band's use of humour and visual performance elements, including earlier imagery associated with the album "Highway to Hell". He additionally recalled being influenced by early film images of Brigitte Bardot. Songs reportedly recorded during the sessions but not included on the album include "Let It Go", "R.I.P. It Up", "Whistle Blower", "Rave On" and "The Cock Crows". The album cover features a bronze statue of Angus Young, which was later replicated as a large prop during the supporting tour. The album produced three singles: "Stiff Upper Lip", "Safe in New York City" and "Satellite Blues". In Australia, New Zealand and Europe, a two-disc tour edition was released in 2001 by Albert Productions. This edition included the album, the B-side "Cyberspace" from "Safe in New York City", five live tracks from "No Bull", and video content for the singles. The music video for "Stiff Upper Lip", directed by Andy Morahan, depicts the band driving a red 1997 Hummer H1, becoming stuck in traffic, and then performing in a street setting. The band is shown listening to "It's a Long Way to the Top (If You Wanna Rock 'n' Roll)" prior to the traffic scene. Following the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks, "Safe in New York City" was included in a Clear Channel memorandum listing songs considered lyrically sensitive, alongside several other AC/DC tracks including "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap", "Shot Down in Flames", "Shoot to Thrill", "Hell's Bells", "T.N.T." and "Highway to Hell". In a 2000 interview with Guitar World, Angus Young stated that "Safe in New York City" was intended as a tongue-in-cheek song, reflecting on public discussions about safety and unpredictability in New York. "Stiff Upper Lip" reached number 7 on the US Billboard 200 and number 12 in the United Kingdom. It reached number 1 in Finland, Sweden, Germany and Austria. Critical reception noted that the album was more favourably received than "Ballbreaker", though some reviews stated that it did not significantly depart from the band's established style. wiki.content: "Who Made Who" is a soundtrack album by the Australian hard rock band AC/DC. It was released on 26 May 1986 as the soundtrack for the Stephen King film "Maximum Overdrive". The album was reissued in 2003 as part of the AC/DC Remasters series. Three tracks on the album – "Who Made Who", "D.T." and "Chase the Ace" – were newly written and recorded specifically for the release. The remaining tracks were previously issued by the band on earlier albums. Only the song "Ride On" features former lead vocalist Bon Scott, who died in 1980, while the other tracks feature his successor Brian Johnson. In conjunction with the album, AC/DC released a 24-minute video compilation containing promotional videos for "Who Made Who", "You Shook Me All Night Long", a remixed version of "Shake Your Foundations", and "Hells Bells", as well as live footage of "For Those About to Rock (We Salute You)" recorded in Detroit in 1983. The music video for the title track, directed by David Mallet, was filmed at the Brixton Academy in London. It features numerous performers portraying clones of guitarist Angus Young. According to "AC/DC: Maximum Rock & Roll", the participants included several hundred fans, many of whom waited overnight outside the venue to take part, including members of the band's UK fan club and individuals who had learned of the event through radio announcements. "Who Made Who" was written for "Maximum Overdrive", a film in which machines become autonomous and hostile toward humans. The song's lyrics address themes related to technology created by humans gaining control over their creators and the resulting reversal of power dynamics. Although "Maximum Overdrive" received negative critical reception and performed poorly at the box office, the soundtrack achieved commercial success. It reached number 16 on the UK Albums Chart and number 33 on the US Billboard 200. The title track became one of the band's most successful singles in several years, reaching the top 10 in Australia and number 16 in the United Kingdom. It was also voted the second-best track of 1986 by readers of Hit Parader magazine. A re-release of "You Shook Me All Night Long" from the album reached number 46 in the UK singles chart. The album has sold approximately five million copies in the United States. Reviewer Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic described the album as a retrospective of AC/DC's work and noted the inclusion of selected tracks from earlier, less successful albums. wiki.content: "Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released on 25 July 1980 by Albert Productions and Atlantic Records. It is the band's first album with Brian Johnson as lead vocalist, following the death of previous singer Bon Scott earlier in 1980. After the commercial success of the 1979 album "Highway to Hell", the band had planned to continue recording material for a follow-up. In February 1980, Bon Scott died in London after a night of heavy drinking. The cause of death was recorded as acute alcohol poisoning and classified as death by misadventure. The group briefly considered disbanding but ultimately decided to continue and recruited Brian Johnson, formerly of the band Geordie, as their new singer. The album was written by Johnson and brothers Angus and Malcolm Young, and produced by Robert John "Mutt" Lange, who had also worked on "Highway to Hell". Recording took place over approximately seven weeks between April and May 1980 at Compass Point Studios in Nassau, Bahamas. The sessions were later mixed at Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The band has stated that the album's all-black cover was intended as a gesture of mourning for Bon Scott, although the record label initially expressed reservations about the design. Prior to joining AC/DC, Brian Johnson was selected after auditions held following Scott's death. He impressed the band during rehearsals and was officially offered the position in March 1980. During the transition period, the band focused on preparing new material, some of which developed from earlier ideas. The recording process was influenced by challenging environmental conditions in the Bahamas, including storms and power disruptions. Johnson has described the sessions as demanding, particularly due to producer Mutt Lange's emphasis on precise vocal performances. Engineer Tony Platt also noted that adapting the studio environment to the band's sound presented difficulties. Several elements contributed to the album's production, including the use of a Schaffer–Vega wireless system to achieve a distinctive guitar sound. A bell sound featured on the opening track "Hells Bells" was ultimately recorded using a custom-made bell after alternative recordings were considered insufficient. The album's title track and other songs reflect themes typical of the band's established style, including high-energy rock arrangements and straightforward lyrical structures. "Back in Black" was released first in the United States in July 1980, followed by releases in Europe and Australia in August of the same year. It achieved immediate commercial success, reaching high chart positions in several countries, including number one in the United Kingdom and number four in the United States. The album remained in the US Top 10 for several months and contributed to renewed interest in the band's earlier catalogue, with previous albums re-entering charts in the UK. In the United States, the earlier album "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap" was also reissued following the success of "Back in Black" and later achieved a higher chart position than the album itself. Music videos were produced for several tracks, including "You Shook Me All Night Long", "Hells Bells", "Back in Black", and "Rock and Roll Ain't Noise Pollution". "You Shook Me All Night Long" became the band's first single to enter the US Top 40, peaking at number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album was supported by a long international tour, which contributed to the band's growing global profile in the early 1980s. Commercially, "Back in Black" became one of the best-selling albums in music history, with estimates of around 50 million copies sold worldwide. In the United States, it has been certified multiple times platinum and is among the highest-selling albums in that market. In 2024 it was certified 27× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, reflecting 27 million units sold in the US. It is also widely cited as one of the best-selling rock albums ever released and one of the most commercially successful albums not to reach number one on the US charts. Critical reception of the album has been mixed but generally positive in retrospective assessments. Some reviewers have described it as a defining hard rock record characterised by its direct production style and consistent songwriting, while others have criticised aspects of its lyrical content and thematic focus. Early reviews varied, with some praising its energy and cohesion and others finding the material repetitive.
